extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of English literature; theater practitioners and general readers of classic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and appreciation of Ben Jonson's play Epicoene and the critical commentary surrounding his dramatic and lyrical craft. Useful for literary students, theater practitioners, and readers studying early-modern English drama and aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of plays: to profit and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ends of all, who for the scene do write, Are, or should be, to profit and delight."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwriting should aim to both instruct/profit and entertain/delight. The prologue elaborates that writers should serve the audience's taste and produce work that provides both enjoyment and moral or intellectual benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cater to diverse audience tastes / provide variety
rubrics_metrics.description: "Be fit for ladies: some for lords, knights, 'squires; Some for your waiting-wench, and city-wires; Some for your men, and daughters of Whitefriars."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play (or author's output) should include variety to suit different social groups and tastes; avoid offering a single, monotonous kind of entertainment ("To present all custard, or all tart... Or to want bread, and salt, were but coarse art").

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid direct application/libel; write 'things (like truths) well feign'd'
rubrics_metrics.description: "On forfeit of yourselves, think nothing true: Lest so you make the maker to judge you... poet never credit gain'd By writing truths, but things (like truths) well feign'd."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base dramatic portrayals on identifiable real persons so as to libel them; strive instead for believable fiction that captures truth without being a direct accusation or literal reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleverness of construction and rising climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for The Alchemist: "utmost cleverness in construction, the whole fabric building climax on climax, witty, ingenious, and so plausibly presented..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotting that accumulates tension and scenes in escalating climaxes and that displays ingenuity in structure is a valued quality, even if it departs from strict realism, provided it remains plausibly presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifelike characterisation and realism drawn from life
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's personages "stand out with such lifelike distinctness"; in comedies of London life he is a "genuine realist, drawing from the life about him with an experience and insight..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be rendered with vivid, distinctive detail and grounded in observation of real life and social types, giving the play a sense of authenticity and intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and inventive comic force
rubrics_metrics.description: "full of the keenest and cleverest of satire and inventive to a degree beyond any English comedy save some other of Jonson's own."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharp, clever satire and inventive comic situations are central virtues; broad or Rabelaisian humour can be effective (as in Bartholomew Fair), but must be handled with skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose tempered by humour and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Jonson and Dickens are described as "moralists, seeking the truth by the exaggerated methods of humour and caricature... but possessed of a true pathos and largeness of heart."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective drama may use exaggeration and caricature to reveal moral truths, but should retain genuine emotional depth and humane feeling rather than mere cynicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint with caricature and avoidance of personal lampoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Late plays "revert to caricature and the hard lines of allegory; the moralist is more than ever present, the satire degenerates into personal lampoon..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caricature and allegory can be useful, but excess risks crude or malicious personal attacks and diminishes artistic merit; satire should avoid sinking into petty lampooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and intertextuality used to improve sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's "theory of authorship involved a wide acquaintance with books and 'an ability ... to convert the substance or riches of another poet to his own use.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly learning and appropriation of earlier authors is a legitimate method when the writer transforms and 'betters' sources—originality may arise from reworking inherited material into superior form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and perfection of literary finish in lyrics
rubrics_metrics.description: His theory demanded "design and the perfection of literary finish... not a word too much or one that bears not its part in the total effect"; yet this can lead to stiffness compared to spontaneous lyricism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyric poetry should show deliberate design, careful craft, concision, and every word contributing to the whole; recognize the tradeoff that excessive polish may reduce spontaneity and emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of form: epigram and occasional verse for pointed wit
rubrics_metrics.description: "Jonson is even better in the epigram and in occasional verse where rhetorical finish and pointed wit less interfere with the spontaneity and emotion..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain forms (epigram, occasional verse) are especially appropriate for Jonson's strengths—brisk, finished, witty pieces—whereas other lyric modes may require more spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, directness, and sense of form in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's prose is "characterised by clarity and vigorous directness, nor is it wanting in a fine sense of form or in the subtler graces of diction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose (dramatic or critical) should aim for clear, vigorous expression and a sense of formal balance and diction that supports meaning and tone.
